analysis.one_liner: Requires financial regulators to prove a rule's benefits exceed its costs before issuing it.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Shelby with 11 Republican cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in September 2011 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced ten federal financial regulators — including the SEC, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, and the new Consumer Financial Protection Bureau — to produce detailed cost-benefit analyses before proposing any rule, and barred them from finalizing any rule whose quantified costs exceeded its quantified benefits. It would have let courts throw out rules that skipped these steps, and required agencies to draw up plans for streamlining or repealing existing regulations. The bill arrived just as regulators were writing the rules to implement the 2010 Dodd-Frank financial overhaul, which had passed after the 2008 financial crisis.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, securities firms, and other financial companies that faced new compliance obligations under post-crisis rules. Requiring agencies to quantify costs and benefits, adding 90-day minimum comment periods, and opening every rule to court challenge would have slowed or stopped many of those rules, and the cost side of the ledger is far easier to quantify than the benefits of prevented fraud or crises.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits a financial regulator from issuing a proposed rule unless it includes a detailed analysis of the need for the rule, why private markets or state regulators could not address the problem, the adverse impacts on regulated entities, and a quantitative and qualitative assessment of all anticipated direct and indirect costs and benefits.

It bars an agency from publishing a final rule if the agency itself determines that the quantified costs are greater than the quantified benefits, though Congress could override that bar with a joint resolution.

It gives anyone 'adversely affected or aggrieved' by a rule one year to sue in federal appeals court over the agency's compliance with the analysis requirements, and the court must vacate the rule if the agency fell short unless the agency shows clear and convincing evidence that vacating it would cause irreparable harm.

It requires each agency to develop and post a plan to 'modify, streamline, expand, or repeal' existing regulations to make its program 'more effective or less burdensome,' and to file five-year retrospective reports on each rule's costs and benefits.

The bill covers ten regulators including the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the SEC, the CFTC, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, and the agencies overseeing Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, and directs the SEC and CFTC to plan for extending the same requirements to their self-regulatory bodies.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers and investors, in the form of delayed or weaker financial rules: the consumer protections, market transparency, and bank oversight being written after the 2008 crisis would each have to clear an analytical and legal gauntlet. Quantified compliance costs are easy to total up, while the benefits of rules that prevent fraud, hidden fees, or systemic risk rarely show up in a number, so the cost test would tend to stop protective rules.

drawbacks.text: The analytical burden is substantial: the bill requires agencies to justify why private markets or state authorities cannot solve the problem, assess alternatives including pilot programs, reproduce their data and methods publicly, and certify uncertainty in every assumption — work that would consume regulator resources and time while Dodd-Frank rulemaking was still pending.

Hard cases would cut against the bill's own test: some worthwhile rules have diffuse, long-term benefits — such as rules reducing the risk of a systemic crash — that cannot be convincingly quantified within the bill's framework, so a rule whose quantified costs exceeded quantified benefits could be legally barred even if its real-world benefits were large.

Supporters argued in effect that post-crisis rulemaking was imposing heavy compliance costs on banks and capital markets without adequate accountability, and that a cost-benefit gate and retrospective review would make regulation more disciplined — a position the bill's 11 Republican cosponsors endorsed by signing on.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some pieces — five-year retrospective reviews, public posting of underlying data, and a requirement to assess whether consumers or small businesses would be disproportionately burdened — are reasonable accountability measures on their own. But the bill's core mechanism weighs the equation the same way in every case: costs to regulated firms are quantified, benefits to the public usually are not, and a rule that fails the arithmetic cannot be finalized. Applied to the regulators writing post-crisis rules, the design skews toward stopping protective regulation rather than merely documenting it, and the private right of action with automatic vacatur would have added a second, litigation-based brake on rulemaking.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in September 2011 and referred to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Shelby introduced the bill on September 22, 2011, joined by 11 Republican cosponsors; it was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote — through the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013.
The bill's sponsors were all Republicans, and it was offered as the Dodd-Frank financial overhaul's rules were still being written by the ten agencies the bill would have covered.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the post-crisis financial rulemaking underway at the SEC, CFTC, Fed, FDIC, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau continued without the bill's cost-benefit gate, 90-day comment requirement, or exposure to court vacatur — so consumers retained the regulatory protections as written, while the banks and securities firms that stood to gain from slower rulemaking did not get the relief the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers kept existing financial rules; banks got no relief

for.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
for.role: U.S. Senator from Alabama; Ranking Member, Senate Banking Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill in the Senate.

against.name: Sen. Tim Johnson
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Did not schedule any committee action on the bill; it sat in the committee with no hearing, markup, or report for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-run Banking Committee gave the bill no action; no Democrat signed on.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed a cost-benefit test, minimum comment periods, and litigation exposure on every rule the banking, securities, and derivatives regulators issued, slowing or blocking the post-crisis rules those firms faced. Consumers and investors would bear the other side of that trade in the form of weaker and later protections.

industries.industry: Financial regulators (CFPB, SEC, CFTC, Fed, FDIC, and others)
industries.note: Ten agencies would have had to produce extensive analyses before any proposed rule, post reproducible data and methods, publish five-year impact reports, and defend rules in court against automatic vacatur. Their ability to write and enforce rules quickly would have been sharply constrained.
